_source.displaydescription:
Trivikrama Viṣṇu temple is located at Haugaḥ Ṭola, in front of the Haugaḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL2670). This temple is on the left side of the road that runs from Mangal Bazar to Lagankhel. It is built upon a double plinth and the principal façade is to the west. The temple can be accessed by climbing a narrow flight of stairs guarded by two small stone lions. The main façade has a single carved door on the ground floor and a surmounting toraṇa supported by the door posts. The other three walls have been left blank and have no openings. The first floor level is distinguished by beautifully carved wooden cornice bands. Four carved windows on the first floor are flanked by two small aedicules, and these can be found on each side of the temple. The overhanging roof is covered with traditional jhĩgaṭī tiles and supported by the carved struts. Some of these struts are missing and have been replaced by plain ones. The temple structure's bell-shaped dome structure above the first roof is unique. This towering octagonal dome has been plastered with lime and has a gilded finial with single layer of āmalaka.

Sixteen struts support the roof of this two-storied temple. Among them, six older struts display carvings of various incarnations of Viṣṇu. The other, newer struts are plain and were fixed in place after the original ones were stolen. A stone statue of Trivikrama Viṣṇu is enshrined in the sanctum of the temple. This form of Viṣṇu is also called Viṣṇu Vikrānta or Vāmana. Viṣṇu has an aura behind his face and is wearing a crown, earrings, a necklace, arm jewelry and a bracelet. He has eight hands, and holds a sword, a wheel and a punishing stick in three of his right hands. The fourth right hand is performing the gesture of varada. On his left, he holds a shield, a conch and a club, whilst his fourth hand is performing a tarjanī gesture. His left leg rises up to the level of his head. The Śrīmadbhāgavatamahāpurāṇa (8.18) states that Viṣṇu descended as the Vāmana to restore the authority of Indra over the heavens, as it had been taken by the benevolent Asura King Mahābali. Vāmana, a dwarf Brahmin, went to the king to request land that he could set his foot upon for three paces. Mahābali promised to provide him with this amount of land. Vāmana then grew himself to gigantic proportions and strode over the three worlds. With his first step, he covered the space from heaven to earth, and with his second he strode from the earth to the netherworld. WIth these steps, Mahābali's realms were covered entirely, and there was no space for him to take his third step. Unable to fulfill his promise, Mahābali offered his head for the third, and so Vāmana placed his foot on Mahabali's head.

No inscription or any other historical document recording the initial construction of the temple could be uncovered. Relying on the architecture of the temple as a dating method, Jośī (VS 2029, 58) assumes that this temple was constructed in the 18th century. Nowadays, the temple is in a neglected condition. There are shops on the temple's plinths, the sanctum is used as a storage room, and the key to the door is in the possession of the shopkeepers.

_source.displaydescription: Local residents refer to this Caitya as Taḥ Gaḥ Bhawāndyaḥ. According to H. Śākya’s (1993, 82) classification, this Caitya is a Vajradhātu Caitya. The Caitya has niches on its eastern, southern, western and northern sides which contain stone statues of Akṣobhaya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amogasiddhi respectively. The stone inscription attached to the western platform has been severely damaged. The Caitya has a guṭhī that consists of five members from the Jyapū community. They have been taking care of the monument and conduct its yearly religious activities.

_source.displaydescription:
Thyākā Bāhāḥ is located near Naka Bahī (LAL0880) to the right-hand side of the street on the way to Kvālkhu. The small courtyard of the Bāhāḥ measures 3.6 m x 3.8 m and is surrounded by residential buildings. The way to access the Bāhāḥ is not immediately obvious; one needs to pass through a shop to reach it.

The courtyard is encircled by a stone plinth and a cement plastered floor. The main temple is a single storey structure built on a raised plinth that is 80 cm high. It is open to the east side, while its rear west wall is attached to the neighbouring building. The main entrance to the shrine has a toraṇa attached to its timber carved frame and is sheltered by an overhanging roof, on top of which is half-domed pinnacle. The toraṇa displays images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara. Two small niches to the south and north of the main shrine house small statues of the Buddhist deities Mañjuśrī and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara respectively. Both niches are topped with prayer wheels. A small statue of Gaṇeśa can be found on the southern wall of the courtyard.

The name of the Bāhāḥ is comes from the name of the ṭola. This is an independent Bāhāḥ; it was constructed by a member of Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra (Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ). Unlike other Bāhāḥs there is no kvāḥpāḥchẽ here. Instead, the shrine of Akṣobhya is attached to the western wall of the courtyard. Inside the sanctum, one can find a marble image of Akṣobhya sitting on two layers of lotus petals. Marble lions were placed on the both sides of the entrance. However, only the northern lion remains today (2019). Inside the courtyard, one can also find a djarmadhātujinālaya caitya (170 cm high). This was installed in 1895 (NS 1015).

No inscription recording the history of the Bāhāḥ could be found.

_source.displaydescription:
Ibāḥ Bahī Dune Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Ibāḥ Bahī (LAL2730) and is situated to its west. This Bāhāḥ can be accessed through the back door of the Ibāḥ Bahī. Alternatively, there are also other two access points: either from the southwest corner, or the northwest corner from Ibāḥ Bahī. Bhājudhana Siṃha from Ibāḥ Bahī constructed this small Bāhāḥ, and so it is also called Bhājudhanasiṃha Vihāra.

The courtyard measures 4 m × 13 m and contains a shrine of Akṣobhya Buddha at its centre. The god house is attached to the western wall of the Ibāḥ Bahī, and measures 3.2 m in width and 2.1 m in depth. It is built in brick masonry and has a flat concrete slab as a roof. The main door of the structure is not centrally aligned with the shrine, and it lacks the artistic features common to Bāhāḥ. The door has some carvings, and is flanked by wall paintings of Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. A small window is fixed to the left-hand side of the main door. Inside the sanctum, there is a north-facing brass image of Akṣobhya. The stone image of the deity was stolen 3-4 years ago, and this new one was installed in its place. On top of the roof, one can find a stūpa-shaped finial.

Images of Hanumān and Mahākāla are attached to the wall and flank the entrance that leads to Ibāḥ Bahī. The Bāhāḥ-courtyard is paved with teliyā bricks and also contains a Pañcāvaliyukta Caitya. No inscription or other document providing information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ could be found. However, Pruscha (1975, 204) dates it to the 19th century.

_source.displaydescription:
Sikucā Bāhāḥ, a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260), is located to the north-east corner of the Thainā crossroad. This bāhāḥ is on the way to Thainā from Saugaḥ Hiti. The bāhāḥ-courtyard is sunken and has an Aśoka Caitya at its center on the axis to the entrance and the main bāhāḥ building. A dharmadhātu maṇḍala is located to the south in front of the caitya. The western wall of the bāhāḥ is attached to a newly constructed five-storied building. Three steps guarded by two small stone lions lead up to the bāhāḥ. Its main entry door is to the north and boasts an original carved door frame with new paneled door leaves. Two small windows on either side of the door are now used as the niches for the māne (prayer wheel). The ground floor is separated from the first floor by a band of carved timber cornice. The principal façade has a central five-fold pāsukājhyāḥ on the first floor; this is flanked by two small aedicules on either side, as is standard. Above the pasukājhyāḥ, one can find seven images of the Buddhist deities with Prajñāpāramitā to their right and Lokeśvara to their left. A projecting slanted balcony with a simple railing of vertical balusters fixed to the timber handrail can be found on the second floor.

The entrance is flanked by concrete statues of Sāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Images of the Five Buddhas, parrots, eight auspicious symbols and other motifs have been carved on the entrance. A small caitya flanked by two deers has been fixed above it. Passing through the entrance, one can see a statue of Gaṇeśa to the right and Mahākāla, Garuḍa and Bhīmasena to the left. All are fixed on the walls of the residential buildings. The north-facing three-storied esoteric shrine (āgama) of the bāhāḥ stands at the south wing of the courtyard. The pinnacle of the bāhāḥ is a stūpa which is located on the ridge of the corrugated galvanized iron sheets roofing. This roof is supported by plain struts. A metal banner hangs down from the pinnacle to the top of the pāsukājhyāḥ. The first floor houses the āgama, whilst the second floor remains empty. The toraṇa above the left window on the first floor has already been lost. The sanctum of the bāhāḥ is located on the ground floor. J. Locke (1985, 103) mentions that there was once a toraṇa with images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara above the entrance of this sanctum. However, this was stolen some years ago. The entrance is flanked by two concrete images of Lokeśvara and two prayer wheels. The steps leading to the sanctum are flanked by two stone lions and metal flags. Inside the sanctum, one can find a stone image of Akṣobhya.

No inscription or other documented evidence with any information about the establishment of the bāhāḥ could be found. A legend suggests that this monastic building's statue of Akṣobhya is related to the Guji Bāhāḥ (LAL2490). The Guji Bāhāḥ complex once caught fire, and the sandalwood statue of its main deity was brought here for its protection. After the fire, in NS 1 (881 CE), a donor named Vaiśravarṇa reconstructed the bāhāḥ. People then came to this bāhāḥ to retrieve the main deity. However, they could not lift the image up; it had become fixed in its place. As such, the image became siddha (established) there, and so it was that this bāhāḥ got the name 'Siddha Bāhāḥ'. Over time, this changed into Sikucā Bāhāḥ (cf. H. Śākya 2001, 29-30). A tradition dictates that initiates of this bāhāḥ must be taken to Guji Bāhāḥ and shown the image of Akṣobhya. J. Locke (ibid.) mentions that a descendant of Abhayarāja (the man who constructed the Mahābuddha Temple (LAL2340)) built the Sikucā Bāhāḥ, though he does not provide any source.

_source.displaydescription:
This monastic compound is a branch of the larger monastery Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440). It has a small shrine on its western side that faces east. This shrine takes the form of a one-storey temple based on a low stone plinth. The main deity has been placed on a raised plinth 90 cm above this base plinth. The plinth has a nāgvaḥ design (quarter round) profile at its base with a band of kasimvaḥ decorative bricks above it. A line of nāgabelī can be found on the brick wall around the middle of the plinth. The edge of the plinth consists of a black stone above a layer of lotus leaf bricks that have eroded due to weather exposure. On top of this plinth is a small carved timber structure which opens up at three sides and with a rear brick wall.

The sanctum has a unique pitched roof; its three tiers are plastered in lime, and the upper part has a bell-shaped design. A stūpa forms the pinnacle of the temple. In front of the temple structure and at the center of the courtyard, one can find a vajradhātu caitya built on a square plan of 386 cm. A small dharmadhātu maṇḍala (80 cm high) has been built between the caitya and the temple structure. The square courtyard measures 13.3 m x 13.3 m and is surrounded by residential buildings in all directions, with a small open space at the south-east corner.

Normally, one can see images of Mahākāla and Hanumān at the gate of most bāhāḥs, however this is not the case here. There is also no toraṇa above the main shrine's entrance. Locke (1985, 159) and Vajrācārya (1993, 117) both mention that the main deity in the sanctum used to be a statue of Amitābha. However, this has been replaced by a stone statue of an eastern-facing Akṣobhya.

No inscription or other document providing any further information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ could be uncovered. Although he cannot find hard evidence to prove his theory, Pruscha (2015, 140) argues that this monument was constructed in the 16th century.

The Bāhāḥ was built by Śreṣṭhas, and Vajrācāryas from Bu Bāhāḥ used to perform the ritual worship in the shrine. The Śreṣṭha representatives bestowed lands upon the shrine to fund a guṭhī for its management (Vajrācārya 1993, 117). Until the late 20th century, 5 pāthī of unhusked rice was collected every year for the Bāhāḥ from the harvest. Today, the situation has changed; the Bāhāḥ no longer receives income from the land and the daily ritual worship has come to an end.

The square courtyard measures 13.3 m x 13.3 m and is surrounded by residential buildings in all directions, with a small open space at the south-east corner.

Normally, one can see images of Mahākāla and Hanumān at the gate of most bāhāḥs, however this is not the case here. There is also no toraṇa above the main shrine's entrance. Locke (1985, 159) and Vajrācārya (1993, 117) both mention that the main deity in the sanctum used to be a statue of Amitābha. However, this has been replaced by a stone statue of an eastern-facing Akṣobhya.

No inscription or other document providing any further information about the establishment of the Bāhāḥ could be uncovered. Although he cannot find hard evidence to prove his theory, Pruscha (2015, 140) argues that this monument was constructed in the 16th century.

The Bāhāḥ was built by Śreṣṭhas, and Vajrācāryas from Bu Bāhāḥ used to perform the ritual worship in the shrine. The Śreṣṭha representatives bestowed lands upon the shrine to fund a guṭhī for its management (Vajrācārya 1993, 117). Until the late 20th century, 5 pāthī of unhusked rice was collected every year for the Bāhāḥ from the harvest. Today, the situation has changed; the Bāhāḥ no longer receives income from the land and the daily ritual worship has come to an end.

_source.displaydescription: The small courtyard in which Vajradhara Phalcā is located is called Ghana Bāhāḥ (LAL2330) and contains a small temple in which a new Akṣobhya Buddha image resides. The temple is flanked by two phalcās: Mahākāla Phalcā (LAL4092) to the south-east and Vajradhara Phalcā to the north-west. Vajradhara Phalcā used to house a Vajradhara statue, however this was stolen around 1985. J. Locke (1985, 112) confirms that the shrine was empty upon his visit. Since the disappearance of the deity, religious activities at the Phalcā have also ceased. The stone stele located behind the stone pedestal has three lines inscribed in Sanskrit. The walls and niches were once plastered. Currently, the Phalcā is used for storing building materials for a house under construction next door. Only its stone pedestal remains.Vajradhara Phalcā is in an advanced state of decay, though it retains many of its original components such as simple carved pillars, a traditional shrine with a historic carved door, and its jingati roof tiles. However, the ridged tiles have been replaced with plain brick and the roof is leaky. The platform’s stone edge on the eastern side appears to have been well-preserved but the tile paving is badly damaged. The original entry door at the east has been replaced by a frame covered in metal.

_source.displaydescription:
Duru Bāhāḥ Nani can be accessed from the northwest corner of the Pimbahal area through a narrow alley under the residential buildings or via a narrow path to the west of the Sulima area. The main shrine has three storeys and faces east.

The principal façade of the main shrine has a main door and two small latticed windows on the ground floor. A threefold pāsukājhyaḥ is on the central axis of the first floor, and has two small-carved windows on either side. Three openings can be found on the second floor above this, though they lack window shutters. The building has been reconstructed using bricks on mud mortar, and is roofed with corrugated metal sheets. Two dharmadhātu maṇḍalas and a vajradhātu caitya are in line with the front of the main building. The courtyard was recently (writing in 2019) paved with hexagonal concrete blocks.

Duru Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ (Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra). Rather than referring to it as a vihāra or bāhāḥ, local people call it Bhagiṃ Nani. A historical photo (see Pruscha 1975, 148) shows that main shrine of the Bāhāḥ once had a tiled roof. Locke  (1985, 128) has described the toraṇa above the entrance of the sanctum as containing images of Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, and Pruscha's photo (1975, 148) confirms this. However, the toraṇa is no longer there.  

Entering the sanctum, one finds an east-facing image of Akṣobhya. The inscription attached to the wall to the south of the entrance informs that this vihāra was established by Ratna Vajrācārya in NS 797 (CE 1677). Locke (ibid.) writes that it was a branch of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ until 1975 and became later a branch of Guji Bāhāḥ. However, local people say that this Bāhāḥ is and has always been a branch of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ. As evidence, they mentioned that a traditional practice takes place on the 10th day of the bright half of the Kārttika. On this day, the feast of the Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ Saṅgha is organised and the bāphāḥcā offers a pumpkin to its branch monasteries among them this Bāhāḥ.
